To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the acylation of short cationic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) can lead to enhanced activity against a variety of target cells, and the length and nature (acetyl, acyl, or aminoacyl) of the acyl group can modulate the activity of the resulting peptide.
acylated peptides are less effective against bacteria and protozoa than the corresponding aminoacyl derivatives.
the acylation of the N terminus of a peptide can be a powerful tool for enhancing its antimicrobial activity.

the design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of novel antimicrobial peptides.
the design of new antimicrobial peptides and the understanding of structure-activity relationships of these molecules.

the design and synthesis of novel antimicrobial peptides, which are characterized by their ability to inhibit the growth of microorganisms and by the fact that they do not show hemolytic activity against human red blood cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antimicrobial properties of the peptide are modulated by the length and the nature of the acyl group, and the effect on the antimicrobial activity is highly dependent on the target cell.

the effect of acylation depends on the peptide and its target, and that acylation can enhance the antimicrobial activity of short peptides, but only if the peptide is not too hydrophobic to start with.
the acylated antimicrobial peptides are not more active than the aminoacyl ones, although their activity is more stable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

acylated short peptides are not always more active against bacteria than their unacylated counterparts and that aminoacylation is a promising approach to enhance the activity of acylated peptides against bacteria.

the acylation of antimicrobial peptides is not only an interesting tool to modulate peptide activity but that the acyl moi-ety can also be used to modulate the peptide's properties in a way that can lead to improved activity against a variety of microorganisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hydrophobicity of the acyl chain is the most important factor in determining the antimicrobial properties of acylated antimicrobial peptides.
the amino end of an antimicrobial peptide can be used to fine-tune the properties of a peptide, and this can be achieved by acylation, which can also be reversed to aminoacylation.
acyl and aminoacyl derivatives of antimicrobial peptides are not interchangeable.
